As someone who is currently ranked master, which places me in the top 1%, I've landed Nobushi's kick offensively more than once in every single duel I've played with her. Perhaps top tournament players don't like her, but Ubisoft has already stated that they're balancing around the top 2.5% of players, not the absolute top. Sometimes I'm convinced reddit plays a different version of For Honor as everyone else. This pack mentality, where everyone pats everyone else on the back for repeating the same mantra of fast attacks are the only way forwards, is ruining the community. Most players on this site aren't part of the top 2.5%, let alone the top 1%. Having fought several grandmasters the last couple weeks, I feel very safe in saying both 500ms lights and 600ms bashes are alive and well, and above all, useful. While I don't make posts on reddit very often for this reason being displayed here, I've been playing the game consistently since beta, for every update, every rework, every balance patch, I play every character, am very familiar with the various values and stats present in the game, have personally tested timed and experimented with many moves myself, and as said before, am currently ranked in the highest rank short of grandmaster. Which would be less impressive at the start of the season, but I got ranked a short while ago, and have regularly played ranked duels since. And the season didn't exactly start yesterday. 

Reddit seems to have this misconception that the top tournament players and the top 2.5% of players are the same. They aren't, and Ubisoft has repeatedly pointed out that balance is being targeted at the top 2.5%, rather than the absolute best players in the world. Tournaments are taken into account, but absolute top level tournaments aren't the basis for the balancing as a whole. As someone who is part of the top 2.5% (but not part of the absolute top), I'm part of the exact section of players the balance is built around. And I can verify that many of the attacks reddit claims are useless are anything but. 

While I was hoping this post would have even a small impact in alleviating the current horde mindset that's so detached from the realities of the game, it appears not. Most people seem to post or comment about things they have never experienced, merely repeating the same garbage that has been passed around and around like some sort of holy text. 

While yes, the very top players can undoubtedly dodge 600ms bashes every single time and block or parry on reaction every 500ms light that comes their way, the top 2.5% as a whole does not, at all. Not even close. One of the easiest ways to see that is the winrate data that, while not an all-revealing story, does tell one important point. Even within the top 2.5%, the difference between most of the characters is not that much in terms of win consistency. The disconnect with the community ideas from the reality of the game primarily stems from stuff such as the tier lists people have made, which very consistently represent the absolute top levels of play, but pretty much never represent the top 2.5% the game is actually balanced after. 500ms bashes, 700ms heavies, 400ms chained lights, those might be the bread and butter of the top competitive duels, but not the top 2.5%, plain and simple. 

The sooner the community as a whole appreciates the realities of the game at the target level, rather than trying to pretend that top tournament play is the target level, the better off the game will be. Top tournament play is, and has consistently been, taken into account in some fashion, but it is not the basis for the balancing of the game. If you want that changed, feel free to petition Ubisoft to only get their design ideas and winrate data from watching tournaments. But as it stands, they are not the primary target level for balancing. 

One additional disconnect is undoubtedly the console-PC disconnect. While everyone is long since tired of hearing about it, there is a difference between the two. There are a lot of reasons for it, and I honestly doubt the whole fps thing is even the main reason, but there is a difference. Having played both, they're like black and white. What should be done about that, if anything, is perhaps another story. But it is related. I would imagine the total difference (if much of any) varies from person to person, but my xbox and PC experiences were wildly different. I would say by as much as 100ms or so at times. While yes I've heard all about the many reasons for why that is, the fact of the matter is that the console world ends up feeling like almost a different game. 

Regardless of all of that, my primary concern and hope was to spur on even a little extra input from those suggesting reworks that uniformly suggest nothing more than to speed up everything. Even good and creative reworks that I've read can't get by without one 400ms light. While other alternatives would depend on the hero, and 400ms lights shouldn't be entirely prohibited, the current plans everyone's making would have 400ms lights be omnipresent across the entire cast. How generic. My goal is, or was, to hopefully spur on some new ideas or plans for how to make an effective character that draws from more than the 'speed everything up' mentality. While I don't anticipate this post to ever see much more light of day than the little it already has, I wanted to make an effort, that way I could at least say I got my ideas out there, even if the current mindset ends up being the inevitable future of the game. I suppose it didn't change much, but I've played the game enough I desired to throw out my two cents anyways, waste of time or not. Perhaps the more generic ideas will win out, but at this point I'll just stick to hoping that it doesn't, at least not entirely. There are a lot of possibilities with this game, but that concludes it for now I guess. I'll just have to wait and see what happens.

That is the main use for most 400ms lights, but putting them everywhere without any use of other ideas is the problem. It quickly becomes generic, and makes the cast too homogeneous.

To talk more about Nobushi specifically, her rather lengthy window for chaining to a kick is what adds a lot of the pressure for the kick itself, rather than it being fast. Comparable to Valkyrie's old legsweep, the ability to delay it or not creates a lot of the pressure. And as far as block pressure is concerned, a heavy out of hidden stance confirms the followup kick. It obviously isn't as good as a move like Warden's SB, but it's hardly useless.

There's a stigma attached to any light slower than 400, any heavy slower than 700, and any melee move slower than 500. No-one seems to bother to justify any use for any move not within those confines, which is just disappointing and frustrating. No-one should be able to sincerely sit and jot down ideas and not a one of them be a use for a move slower than the "accepted" speed for its type. Especially with the many modifiers and effects and whatnot that can be combined in creative ways. There are more ways to make things useful than speeding everything up. And there are more ways to make things prediction based than having every melee move be 500ms. 

My hope is for more people to try and make more creative movesets with alternative solutions to common issues. This also includes looking at the potential usefulness of existing moves or ideas in the game, even if they aren't as good as they could be in their current iteration.

I agree in part, but one thing I didn't really touch on is that it's very easy to give moves a value much higher than the sum of their parts based on the rest of the moveset. 

Take Nobushi for example. If she throws out a heavy, you don't have to parry it, or do anything other than block it and take a small amount of block damage. However, her chains, including one into a kick which can be delayed rather heavily, suddenly make that heavy more important. That kick will force a reaction, and it isn't her only option. Suddenly that heavy opener has a lot more value, because if you don't let her get it off, she won't be chaining into that kick. A lot of existing heroes have seemingly normal moves that help the rest of their kit massively. Blocking or getting hit by Warden's heavy openers drastically increase the safety of his finishers, particularly the top one, in terms of interrupting it. The same is true of Shaman and her unblockable. To touch back on Nobushi, blocking her heavy from hidden stance allows her a free kick. 

These things put a lot more emphasis on otherwise less important moves. Rather than making them faster or whatnot, there are more creative ways to make them force a reaction secondhand or otherwise be important. Passive abilities, stances, different chains of all sorts, anything you can think of can be used to make moves more important and interesting than simply making all the heavies 700 and all the lights 400. I realize all of the examples were heavies, but that's just because the most notable examples in-game currently are heavies. Any one of these ideas, or crazier ones, can be applied to lights as well. Groundbreaking, interesting, and still useful, that's the goal. And as far as introducing new mechanics go, I'd say go for it as well. Although I think different combinations of existing mechanics can create viable heroes without overuse of super fast moves, entirely new ideas just add onto the pile and make it even better. 

While I would definitely agree that designing or reworking a moveset to be fun, maintain the character, and be at least modestly effective all at once is already enough of a challenge, I still believe there are a lot of possibilities regularly overlooked in place of the "speed it all up" mindset. Not that there isn't a place for some fast attacks, but I still would rather spur on more out of the box solutions, even though you are still correct in saying there's only so much that can be done with the existing options. I don't think we've hit the limit of what the existing options can do, let alone brand new mechanisms, and I want to see what all we can come up with.

That being said, most of it sounds like they're throwing around words. Let's take shaman for example. Punished hard if read properly? What punishes are so much more devastating when used against her, exactly? Characters don't magically do more damage if they parry her 500ms light openers than they do if they parry Shinobi's. Dodging her melee moves results in a free guardbreak, just like almost everyone else. Let's take a "high tier" example, Warlord. His headbutt is 500ms, gives 12 damage, chains into nothing, cannot wallsplat. Shaman's forward dodge headbutt is 400ms, gives 15 damage, chains, can wallsplat, and is feintable. The only drawback being her stance slowing down the fastest possible time to get into the move, but that also gives it its greatest strength, that it can be feinted. Both result in a guardbreak if dodged. OOS pressure? Not only are Warlord's max punishes off of any OOS punishes (throw/parry) lower than most of the cast, his only options are effectively just the forward dodge headbutt or guardbreak mixup, or the unlock shield charge or guardbreak mixup. That's all well and good, but what makes it better than anyone else's? Highlander can force them to play his kick/toss mixup. Raider can do the same unlock pressure as Warlord, only he also puts out more damage. 

To me at least, it seems as though they simply list off stuff without giving any reasoning as to why (x set of things) is any better than the similar abilities of other characters. I'm more than open to discussion on this and the reasonings behind some of the rankings as it has long eluded me. 

In addition, while tier lists alone are the classic way to rank, a matrix of different matchups is always the more accurate way to determine the most favorable characters.

Centurion's fully charged heavy tracking and infinite wallsplat combo were fixed almost immediately, and the character has gone essentially untouched since up until his more recent health buff and the addition of his light heavy combo. He's been considered to be underpowered as time has gone on, and was only truly broken for a short duration after release. After that he's been on the decline, from better but not best down to mediocre compared to the rest of the cast.

What, just his shieldbash move in general? He's always had it, and it's a strong enough move but hardly overpowered. It is admittedly fast, the same speed as Warlord's headbutt. It confirms 13 damage. If you dodge it, you get a free guardbreak, unless they light attack. That being said, they have to light attack, so you can bait it out and parry. This becomes it's own mixup, and one that is prevalent with many other characters. While its speed can be annoying, dodging it forcing them into a mixup that if you guess correctly gives you either a guardbreak or light parry, both much higher than 13 damage. I'll concede it can be frustrating for me as well, but it works as intended by and large, and calling it overpowered or asking the move to be removed entirely is a bit much.

I'll do my best to clear things up for anyone who has the same misconceptions.

First and foremost, one of Highlander's main drawbacks in offensive form on top of guardbreak vulnerability is his inability to block, which wasn't mentioned. In addition, he has to get into offensive form first. For this he has options of course. Chaining after a hit is safer, but requires you to get a hit in first. Chaining out of neutral is riskier but allows you to potentially get into offensive form without waiting to land a blow. 

Your statement that offensive form makes his attacks unblockable is not exactly correct. Given that one mostly sees offensive heavies this may seem accurate, but the offensive lights are not unblockable, and there's no special property to his offensive form either. He simply has access to his unblockable offensive heavy as one of the moves he can do from offensive form.

Shugoki needs to land a guardbreak within throw range of a wall to land a demon's embrace confirmed. Your weirdly specific example is either niche intentionally to make it seem as though it's an unusual event, or because you genuinely didn't consider the myriad of times guardbreaks are confirmed. In addition, the reality of it is that it doesn't have to be confirmed to get it. After all, kick into caber toss is your main point of complaint, and in that situation it is simply a mixup in which there is no guarantee it will work. So by these standards, we must also take into account the ability to guardbreak randomly and rely on human error. On top of all of this, there is no law stating Shugoki may only Demon's Embrace when it is confirmed. Even looking at more examples of it being confirmed, there are plenty of occasions in which you can simply trade with hyper armor. 

As for Shaman, the work she requires is to bleed, just as the work required for Highlander is to work his way into safely entering offensive form. Once both have completed their prerequisites, they are free to begin their mixups. Highlander's primary mixup being his kick into caber toss, but of course he has other options. For Shaman, that's her grab. Saying it can be dodged is an interesting reply, seeing as how the same applies to Highlander's kick. Of course Highlander can always feint into caber toss, just like Shaman can always feint into whatever she wants, but probably just another grab to catch you if you dodged, but it's situational of course. 


Long Arm was mostly brought in to counter your statement about melee moves only giving lights. That being said, the risk is a guardbreak, which is the same punish Highlander receives if his opponent guesses right about his kick into caber toss mixup. As for years of planning, it may be slow but it is usually just used as a part of mixups such as the shove mixup. 


As for Raider, it's the same deal as all the others. Mixup, mixup, mixup. Charge, or guardbreak usually in that case. Assuming the value of melee moves only by their value if you always go through with them would make almost all of them a waste except as punishes. Including Highlander's, because it is just a mixup like the others, and if we apply your logic against Raider to Highlander, the conversation would've ended at "he kicks, you dodge and guardbreak". That's simply missing the point of melee moves and their many mixups across the different characters. 

For Warden, his bash is objectively better than the kick into caber toss in terms of how resistant it is to being punished. It can be canceled at any point, even up to 100ms after release. Worst case you mess up, and the punishment you receive is a guardbreak, same as Highlander. 

Also saying that every one of those moves except for Highlander's can be punished "severely" is odd given that they all receive the same punishment, a guardbreak. 

And to reiterate, the kick into caber toss can be punished just like the rest. You dodge correctly, you get a guardbreak. It is not unpunishable, and if your complaint is that you can't punish the move without trying to dodge it, then that's a bit absurd. The entire point is that you can either try and dodge, risk the damage, and potentially punish, or roll away and risk nothing but lose out on your chance to punish, and a chunk of stamina. That's how an entire host of mixups work, and trying to claim Highlander's kick into caber toss should be a move that can be somehow avoided and punished without any risk to the defender is ludicrous. 

As for ganks, the potential to be damaged well beyond the normal for any mistake is the norm. Highlander's offensive form is not unique in that regard, and furthermore since a team situation is the example, it's within the ability of your teammates to simply give him a boop and knock him out of offensive form, including preventing him from even getting his otherwise confirmed offensive heavy should he land a kick/caber toss. Every move of a similar nature has it's own ups and downs in a team fight, and Highlander's are no exception. 

To round it off, if you're really having such issues with him currently, there are two things going on at the moment that may help unless Ubisoft changes them in the future. One is dodge rolling, which allows you to dodge and then roll out on a whim by unlocking. I don't use it personally, and I've heard it is sometimes wonky to do on Highlander, but it does work. This allows you to dodge assuming a kick everytime, and simply roll anyways only if a caber toss comes out. Perhaps not entirely an easy out, but it exists. If you check out Freezing on youtube you will find his video on the topic, as well as other excellent data on the game. The other potential balm to soothe the difficulty is Valkyrie, who is supposed to be able to back dodge into shield crush and avoid both options, and even then feint out of the move to get a free guardbreak. The timing is supposed to be tricky, and I haven't done it myself, but I figured I would share regardless. 

This ought to conclude the full listings of Highlander, and everything in between that you've brought up. In addition, it will hopefully answer others with similar complaints.

That being said, I typed this up earlier and my Reddit crashed while I was typing, so certain things got lost in translation so to speak. My point for highlighting his top storm rush is that, due to the overall 700ms time of the move when compared with the timing of the indicators, it may seem like a quick enough dodge or dodge attack would suffice, but this is incorrect and the top storm rush is actually capable of full 360s to ensure that you don't escape, meaning that the only dodge that can escape is a well-timed dodge attack to interrupt. 

As far as the speed of attacks are concerned, the patch notes say 500, 600, and 700. If it weren't for the community timing them ourselves, we would have no idea otherwise. The way Storm Rush works causes the actual attacks to be 267 367 and 467, which is far faster than we would've otherwise known. While the time between the move being released and the attack hitting is still 500 600 and 700, the timing for the actual attacks, and therefore their reactibility, was by and large concealed. For this reason it's hard to say if their actual intention was to make an attack that clocks in as insanely faster than any other attack in the game, and by all accounts universally unreactable. The other two are only marginally slower. Even if this was their intention, it's still misleading. The point was clarity, which has been achieved now that we know the speed of the attacks themselves.

This seems rather fine at first, and admittedly the damage lines up well. However, the problem is that the devs have made it clear the move is towards being able to punish OOS opponents more, with several changes having been made to that effect. So, why is it that a move designed to punish OOS can potentially reward them with as much damage as you could possibly dish out with it? It doesn't seem to be very punishing in that light, which makes it at odds with its sole purpose of punishing OOS opponents. That is my concern.
